questions.question: How do you send query parameters and authentication with Python Requests?
questions.title: Query Parameters and Authentication with Requests
questions.direct_answer: Pass query parameters through params= so Requests encodes them into the URL. Use auth= for supported authentication handlers or an Authorization header for a bearer token. Keep credentials out of source code and usually out of query strings because URLs are widely logged.

interviewer_intent.testing: Correct placement of query inputs, credentials, headers, and request bodies.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Building query strings by hand or placing secrets in source code and logs.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why 401 and 403 are different outcomes and why HTTPS does not prevent endpoint logging.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: params={...} safely builds the URL query string.
auth=(username, password) applies HTTP Basic authentication.
Bearer tokens normally use Authorization: Bearer <token>.
Load secrets from a secret store or environment, not source code.
A 401 means valid authentication is missing; a 403 means access is refused.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Query parameters describe which result the caller wants, such as a page number, limit, or filter. Authentication proves who the caller is. In Requests, those values should stay separate: ordinary URL inputs go through `params=`, while credentials use `auth=` or the authentication header required by the API.

A call such as `requests.get(url, params={"page": 2, "status": "open"})` percent-encodes the names and values and appends them to the URL. This avoids mistakes with spaces, ampersands, Unicode, repeated values, or a URL that already contains a query string.

For HTTP Basic authentication, `auth=(username, password)` is the clear shorthand. A bearer-token API normally expects `headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"}`. These forms are not interchangeable: the server contract defines the scheme and wire format. Query-string credentials should be used only when that contract leaves no safer option.

The example loads its token at runtime, prepares an order request, and prints only the URL and authentication scheme. `prepare()` performs Requests' URL and header construction but sends no network traffic. A real call should also set a timeout and handle status, decoding, and response validation after dispatch.

support.title: Prepare a filtered bearer request without sending it
support.code:
import os
import requests

def build_orders_request(base_url: str, page: int):
    token = os.environ["ORDERS_API_TOKEN"]
    request = requests.Request(
        "GET",
        f"{base_url}/orders",
        params={"page": page, "status": "open"},
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"},
    )
    return request.prepare()

prepared = build_orders_request("https://api.example.com", 2)
print(prepared.url)
print(prepared.headers["Authorization"].split()[0])
support.caption: Preparing exposes the encoded URL and header shape for testing without contacting an API.

beats.recallRule: Put filters in params, credentials in the documented auth mechanism, and secrets outside source code.

sections.title: URL parameters, headers, and authentication data
sections.content:
An HTTP request has separate locations with separate semantics. The path identifies a resource, the query refines the request, headers carry metadata such as credentials and accepted media types, and the body carries a representation for methods that use one. Mixing these locations makes caching, logging, and security harder to reason about.

Requests accepts lists and repeated query values through params= and performs percent encoding. Passing a prebuilt URL string can work, but manual concatenation easily mishandles spaces, ampersands, Unicode, or an existing query string.

Authentication is defined by the server's scheme. Basic credentials can use auth=. Bearer tokens typically use the Authorization header. OAuth token acquisition and refresh require an OAuth-aware client; adding the word Bearer does not implement that lifecycle by itself.

Secret storage and secret transport are different. A token can be safely loaded from a secret manager yet accidentally exposed by debug logging. Clients should redact Authorization, cookies, and sensitive query fields in traces.

sections.title: Put each value in the right request part
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  I[Client inputs] --> Q[Query: filters, page, limit]
  I --> H[Headers/auth: credentials and metadata]
  I --> B[Body: submitted representation]
  Q --> R[HTTP request]
  H --> R
  B --> R
```

sections.title: Worked Python example
sections.content:
```python
import os
import requests

def list_orders(base_url: str, page: int) -> dict:
    token = os.environ["ORDERS_API_TOKEN"]
    response = requests.get(
        f"{base_url}/orders",
        params={"page": page, "status": "open"},
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"},
        timeout=(3.05, 10),
    )
    response.raise_for_status()
    return response.json()
```

questions.question: When should credentials use auth=, the Authorization header, or a query parameter?
questions.title: Choosing Where API Credentials Belong
questions.direct_answer: Follow the API's authentication scheme: use auth= for Requests-supported handlers such as Basic Auth, use the Authorization header for bearer tokens, and use a query parameter only when the API explicitly requires it. The server contract decides the format; security practice decides how the secret is stored and logged.

interviewer_intent.testing: Matching auth=, Authorization, or query placement to the server's authentication scheme.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Moving credentials to an unsupported location because it appears safer or more convenient.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Separate protocol format from secret storage, expiry, scope, and rotation.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Use auth= for an authentication handler such as HTTP Basic or Digest.
Use Authorization: Bearer for APIs that accept bearer access tokens.
Do not invent a credential location; follow the API specification.
Query-string credentials are more likely to appear in logs and history.
HTTPS is required for credentials, but safe storage and redaction are still needed.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Credential placement is part of the authentication protocol, not a Python style choice. Read the API documentation and reproduce its scheme. Moving the same text between `auth=`, an `Authorization` header, and `params=` changes the HTTP message and usually makes authentication fail.

Use `auth=(user, password)` when the server documents HTTP Basic authentication. Requests turns that tuple into a Basic authorization value during request preparation. Other schemes may use an auth object, such as `HTTPDigestAuth`, because an authentication handler can calculate or modify the outgoing request rather than merely store a string.

For an OAuth-style bearer access token, the usual form is `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, supplied through `headers=` or a client library that manages token refresh. Passing that token as the username in `auth=` would create Basic authentication instead. A signed or custom scheme should use its documented client or `AuthBase` handler.

Use a query parameter only when the API requires it. URLs commonly pass through gateway logs, monitoring tools, support traces, and browser history. HTTPS protects traffic in transit but does not stop endpoints recording the URL. Redact the field and rotate the key when the old contract cannot be changed.

The offline example prepares one Basic request and one bearer request. Both end with an `Authorization` header, but the schemes are different. This is why the decision begins with the server contract; a secret value alone does not tell Requests which authentication protocol to apply.

beats.recallRule: Follow the API scheme first; then protect storage, transport, logging, expiry, and rotation.

sections.title: Authentication schemes decide where credentials belong
sections.content:
Requests prepares authentication before dispatch. An auth handler can modify the outgoing PreparedRequest, which supports more than simply inserting a static header. That distinction matters for challenge-response or signed schemes.

Authorization is the conventional HTTP field for credentials that authorize access to a target. Bearer is only one scheme. The value format, token lifetime, scopes, refresh behavior, and audience are defined outside the basic header syntax.

URL query values are part of the target URI. Even with encrypted transport, infrastructure at either endpoint may record that URI. This larger exposure surface is why credentials should not be moved into the query unless the contract requires it.

sections.title: Credential placement decision
sections.content:
| API contract says | Requests form | Main boundary |
|---|---|---|
| HTTP Basic/Digest | auth= handler | Use HTTPS; protect username/password |
| Bearer access token | Authorization header | Expiry, scope, rotation, redaction |
| API key in query | params= only if required | URL can be logged widely |
| Custom signed scheme | AuthBase/client library | Signing and replay rules are scheme-specific |

sections.title: Worked Python example
sections.content:
```python
import requests

basic = requests.Request(
    "GET", "https://example.com/private", auth=("ada", "secret")
).prepare()
assert basic.headers["Authorization"].startswith("Basic ")

token = "example-token"
bearer = requests.Request(
    "GET",
    "https://example.com/private",
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"},
).prepare()
assert bearer.headers["Authorization"] == "Bearer example-token"
```

questions.question: Why should API keys not be hard-coded or logged, and how should Python load them?
questions.title: Safe API Key Handling in Python
questions.direct_answer: Hard-coded keys enter source history and copied builds, while logged keys spread into systems with broad access and long retention. Python should receive secrets at runtime from a managed secret store or deployment environment, fail clearly when missing, redact them from logs, and support rotation.

interviewer_intent.testing: The complete secret lifecycle from storage and runtime delivery to redaction and rotation.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Deleting a visible key after exposure without revoking it or cleaning its wider copies.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Treat environment variables as a delivery interface rather than a complete secret-management system.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Never commit an API key, even in a private repository or sample config.
Prefer a managed secret store; an environment variable is a simple runtime interface.
Fail at startup when a required secret is absent instead of sending an empty credential.
Redact Authorization, Cookie, and sensitive query values from logs.
Rotate exposed keys and remove them from history; deleting one line is not enough.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
An API key is a credential, not application source. A hard-coded key can remain in Git history, old branches, build artifacts, container layers, backups, and developer machines after the visible line is deleted. Logging creates another copy in systems that often have broad readership and long retention.

A deployment can inject `ORDERS_API_TOKEN`, and Python can read it with `os.getenv()`. Treat the environment as a delivery interface, not as proof that storage is secure: the platform still needs access control and rotation. Reject a missing or blank value before the application starts sending requests.

Attach the token only to the header or parameter required by the API. Logs can record the method, safe path, status, elapsed time, and server request ID without recording `Authorization`, cookies, sensitive query values, or full prepared headers. Redaction must happen before data enters the logging pipeline.

The example validates the environment value, prepares a bearer request, and prints only safe request details. It sends no traffic and never prints the token. Local development may use an ignored secret file, but a real key must not be committed inside a sample `.env` file.

If a key is exposed, revoke or rotate it first; deleting a line or hiding a log view does not invalidate existing copies. Then remove retained copies where practical, review access, and add a guard against recurrence. Least privilege and short lifetimes reduce the damage if prevention fails.

support.title: Load, validate, attach, and redact an API token
support.code:
import os
import requests

def required_secret(name: str) -> str:
    value = os.getenv(name, "").strip()
    if not value:
        raise RuntimeError(f"required secret {name} is not configured")
    return value

token = required_secret("ORDERS_API_TOKEN")
prepared = requests.Request(
    "GET",
    "https://api.example.com/orders",
    params={"status": "open"},
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"},
).prepare()

print(prepared.method, prepared.url)
print("Authorization: [redacted]")
support.caption: The secret reaches the prepared header, while the program's output contains only safe metadata.

beats.cue: Describe the first action after a credential is exposed
beats.spokenText: If a key is exposed, revoke or rotate it first; deleting a line or hiding a log view does not invalidate existing copies. Then remove retained copies where practical, review access, and add a guard against recurrence. Least privilege and short lifetimes reduce the damage if prevention fails.
beats.recallRule: Inject secrets at runtime, expose them only to the request, redact them before logging, and rotate any leaked value.

sections.title: A secret's path from configuration to request
sections.content:
Secret handling has four stages: storage, delivery, use, and replacement. A managed store protects the value at rest and controls who can retrieve it. Deployment delivers it to the process. The application keeps exposure small during use. Rotation replaces it without a source-code release.

Logs are a frequent accidental exit path. HTTP debug tooling may record complete URLs or headers, and exception messages may include prepared requests. Redaction must happen before data enters the logging pipeline, not only in the user interface that displays logs.

Least privilege limits damage when prevention fails. A key should have only the scopes, environments, and lifetime needed by that client. Short-lived access tokens are often preferable when the API and identity platform support them.

sections.title: A secret's safe path
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  S[Secret manager] --> D[Deployment injects runtime value]
  D --> P[Python process]
  P --> H[Authentication header]
  P -. redacted .-> L[Logs and traces]
  R[Rotation] --> S
```

sections.title: Worked Python example
sections.content:
```python
import os
import requests

def required_secret(name: str) -> str:
    value = os.getenv(name, "").strip()
    if not value:
        raise RuntimeError(f"required secret {name} is not configured")
    return value

token = required_secret("ORDERS_API_TOKEN")
session = requests.Session()
session.headers["Authorization"] = f"Bearer {token}"
# Log the URL, method, status, and request ID—not session.headers.
```
